answer:
**Perfect ordering can coexist with very wrong probabilities.** Give two positive examples scores 0.02 and 0.02 and two negatives scores 0.01 and 0.01. Every positive outranks every negative, so the probability that a random positive beats a random negative is one: ROC-AUC=1. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html)

Yet the model claims that cases scored 0.02 succeed only about 2% of the time, while both examples in that group are positive. Its probability estimates are badly mismatched to this observed sample.

**Compute the loss.** Each positive contributes $-\log0.02\approx3.912$, and each negative contributes $-\log0.99\approx0.01005$. Averaging gives about 1.961. A constant prediction of 0.5 has log loss about 0.693, so the perfectly ranking model is much worse under log loss.

A monotonic calibration map can change probability scale while preserving ranking. However, fitting a map perfectly to these four points does not establish calibration on future data. Use separate calibration and test sets with representative prevalence. Choose metrics according to use: ranking candidates, estimating expected value, and making probability-threshold decisions impose different requirements. AUC alone cannot certify the latter two.

**Technical details and references.**

Take labels $(1,1,0,0)$ with predictions $(0.02,0.02,0.01,0.01)$. Every positive outranks every negative, so ROC-AUC is exactly one. But the probabilities are severely underconfident for positives. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html)

$$logloss=-\tfrac14[2\log0.02+2\log0.99]\approx1.961.$$

The constant 0.5 predictor has log loss about 0.693, so the perfectly ranking model is worse under this probability score. Calibration checks frequency conditional on predicted probability, not ranking. A monotone calibration map can preserve AUC while improving probability quality. Use separate calibration data and test distribution; perfectly fitting a calibration map to these four observed points would not establish generalization.
